newsitem.title: UK: GOLF-EUROPEAN TEAM HAS SETTLED LOOK.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-EUROPEAN TEAM HAS SETTLED LOOK.

text.p: The European Ryder Cup team, having survived slight scares about Colin Montgomerie and Bernhard Langer last week, is shaping up as a formidable fighting force less than four months from their defence against the Americans.
Captain Seve Ballesteros, his fanciful objective of being a playing captain rapidly receding, at least can derive satisfaction from the way his storm troops are massing for the battle at Valderrama.
Most of the long-time stalwarts appear ready for yet another Cup encounter at the southern Spanish course from September 26 to 28.
Montgomerie, after his slowest start to a season in recent years, has shown signs of stirring at last.

His victory in the European zone of the Andersen Consulting world championship last month showed a welcome rediscovery of his putting prowess which was missing during an unsuccessful foray onto the U.S. Tour in April.
Then he rebounded from a near disastrous third round of 76 in the British PGA Championship at Wentworth with a week's-best 64 to grab fifth spot in that prestigious event.
Mystery surrounded his withdrawal from last week's European Tournament Players Championship (TPC) which he announced only as being "for personal reasons".
But he quickly scotched the notion that it could be something more serious by entering this week's European Grand Prix at Slaley Hall in the north of England.

He sees it as essential preparation for the U.S. Open at the Congressional Club near Washington next week, less for collecting Ryder Cup points of which he already has enough for selection even if he did not play another qualifying event between now and August 31.

Conventional wisdom has it that 350,000 points will be needed to ensure qualification for the bienniel match and Montgomerie, who won the first qualifying event last September, the European Masters, had just under 400,000 already.

That is some 47,000 behind British PGA champion and points leader Ian Woosnam, who is enjoying a surge in form this year that has brought him back into the top 20 in the world rankings, which he led for several months after his 1991 U.S. Masters triumph.

The other man safely past the projected points minimum and ready for a Ryder Cup debut is Northern Ireland's burly Darren Clarke, who has consolidated his bid with three top-five finishes in the last five weeks.

Fourth just outside the required figure is another veteran on the crest of a wave, German Bernhard Langer, the object of the other scare story last week when he missed the TPC halfway cut because of a back injury.

But Langer reported later the injury was not serious, should heal quickly and would not prevent him continuing towards qualification as well as chasing a new goal of being European number one for the year.

The 39-year-old German, who missed the now-famous crucuial putt at Kiawah Island in 1991, virtually ensured his place in a ninth successive Cup with his successive wins in the Italian and Benson and Hedges International Opens last month.
By doing so, he neatly disposed of suggestions that he might not automatically qualify for selection and might need a wild card to get onto the European team.
Spain's Miguel Angel Martin continues to defy suggestions that he is a potentially weak link in the team, despite his victory early this year in the Heineken Classic in Perth.
The diminutive Spaniard still holds fifth place after a series of solid performances and despite predictions that his game may be too lightweight for the Ryder Cup, he has strong supporters too.
One is Jose Maria Olazabal, his compatriot who is on the fringe of qualifying.
"He never gives up. He may have to use a longer club that other players but he has all the tools and what has changed is his mentality. He believes more in himself," Olazabal said during the PGA.
Martin has missed only one cut since his victory in Perth and in the last two weeks placed joint 19th in the PGA and, after a swing change in mid-tournament, joint fifth at the TPC.

The next three on the list, Per-Ulrik Johansson of Sweden, Dane Thomas Bjorn and voluble Italian Costantino Rocca should hang on to their positions, though Bjorn, seeking his first appearance, and Rocca need to find some spark.
Britons Lee Westwood, who would also be a rookie if he makes it, and 1991 Cup player Paul Broadhurst are ninth and 10th and in those last two positions are vulnerable.
Particularly because the player right behind them is Olazabal, who has battled back successfully from the foot ailment that kept him out of the game for 18 months.
He has won once with five other top-12 finishes in his eight tournaments since beginning his comeback late in February.

Three other experienced Cup men, Britons Sam Torrance, David Gilford and Mark James, who all won singles matches in the 1995 victory at Oak Hill, are between 12th and 20th in the list and could promote themselves by winning in the next few months.

Then there is Nick Faldo, who leaped from 62nd to 20th with his joint second place finish in the PGA and who, though based on the U.S. Tour, has five more counting events to qualify by right and is expected to do so.
That leaves Ballesteros, who has insisted all year that he was on the cusp of turning into something resembling his former greatness - until last week.
Then after missing his eighth cut in 10 events this year at the TPC and dropping to 39th on the list, he said he would not play this week and did not known when he might reappear on the Tour.
He might just have sounded the death knell to his Ryder Cup playing dream.
